body.intro: Friction is the contact force parallel to a surface that opposes sliding, or the tendency to slide, between two solid bodies. It decides whether objects start to move, how fast they accelerate and how steep a slope they can rest on, so it appears in almost every mechanics problem.

sections.heading: Normal force and friction: two parts of one contact force
sections.body:
When two solids touch, the surface pushes back on the body. We split this contact force into two components. The normal force $F_N$ acts perpendicular to the surface and stops the body sinking into it. The frictional force $F_f$ acts parallel to the surface, in the plane of contact, and opposes the sliding (or the tendency to slide) of the body relative to the surface.

On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, $F_N = mg$. This is not always the case: on a slope, or if you also push down or pull up, $F_N$ changes. Always find $F_N$ from the forces perpendicular to the surface.

Friction does not always slow things down. It acts against relative motion between the surfaces, so it can also push a body forwards, as it does on the soles of your shoes when you walk. The diagram shows a block pushed to the right and sliding at constant speed.

figure.alt: A block on a horizontal surface sliding to the right at constant speed. Weight W points down, normal force N points up with equal length, applied force F points right, and friction Ff points left with the same length as F.

check.stem: In the diagram the block slides to the right. What is the direction of the frictional force on the block?

options.text: To the left, parallel to the surface
options.why_wrong: This is correct.

options.text: To the right, parallel to the surface
options.why_wrong: Friction opposes the sliding of the block relative to the surface, so it cannot point in the direction of motion here.
A force perpendicular to the surface is the normal force, not friction.
Downwards is the direction of the weight; friction acts parallel to the surface.

check.feedback_right: Friction acts parallel to the surface and opposes the relative sliding, so it points left.
check.feedback_wrong: Friction lies in the plane of contact and opposes the relative sliding. The block slides right, so friction points left.

sections.heading: Static friction: a limit, not a fixed value
sections.body:
If you push a heavy box gently and it does not move, friction is balancing your push. Static friction adjusts itself to match the applied force, up to a maximum:

$F_f \le \mu_s F_N$

where $\mu_s$ is the coefficient of static friction. It has no units and depends on the two surfaces. The value $\mu_s F_N$ is the largest static friction the surfaces can provide. Below it, $F_f$ equals the force trying to cause sliding (Newton's first law, since the body is in equilibrium). Once the push exceeds $\mu_s F_N$, the body starts to slide.

So for a body at rest you cannot just use $F_f = \mu_s F_N$. Use it only when the body is on the point of slipping. Otherwise, find friction from the force balance.

check.stem: A 5.0 kg block rests on a horizontal table. The coefficient of static friction is 0.40. A horizontal push of 12 N is applied and the block stays at rest. Determine the frictional force on the block, in N.
check.feedback_right: The block is in equilibrium, so static friction equals the 12 N push.
check.feedback_wrong: The block is not moving, so friction equals the applied force: 12 N. Typing 19.6 means you used the maximum value $\mu_s F_N$, which only applies when the block is about to slip.

sections.heading: Dynamic friction and the friction graph
sections.body:
Once a body slides, the frictional force has a constant value given by

$F_f = \mu_d F_N$

where $\mu_d$ is the coefficient of dynamic (kinetic) friction. For most pairs of surfaces $\mu_d < \mu_s$, so it takes more force to start a body moving than to keep it moving. In this model dynamic friction does not depend on the speed or on the contact area.

The graph shows friction against applied force for a block of weight 50 N on a horizontal surface. Friction rises with the applied force while the block is at rest (static friction matching the push). It reaches a peak, the maximum static friction. When the block starts to slide it drops to a lower constant value, the dynamic friction.

figure.alt: Graph of friction force in newtons against applied force in newtons. Friction rises in a straight line from 0 to a peak of 20 N at an applied force of 20 N, then drops to 15 N and stays constant at 15 N as the applied force increases to 40 N.

check.stem: The block in the graph has weight 50 N and rests on a horizontal surface, so $F_N$ = 50 N. Determine the coefficient of dynamic friction.
check.feedback_right: Dynamic friction is the constant 15 N, so $\mu_d = 15/50 = 0.30$.
check.feedback_wrong: Use the flat part of the graph (sliding): $\mu_d = F_f/F_N = 15/50 = 0.30$. An answer of 0.40 comes from using the 20 N peak, which gives $\mu_s$; 0.75 comes from dividing 15 by 20 instead of by $F_N$.

sections.heading: Friction on a slope
sections.body:
On an incline of angle $\theta$ the weight has two components: $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope. The normal force balances the second one, so

$F_N = mg\cos\theta$

Note that $F_N$ is smaller than $mg$. If the body is at rest, static friction acts up the slope and equals $mg\sin\theta$. The body is on the point of slipping when this equals the maximum static friction:

$mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\tan\theta = \mu_s$

The mass cancels. If the slope is steeper than this angle the body slides. Once it slides, friction is $\mu_d mg\cos\theta$ and the resultant force down the slope is $mg\sin\theta - \mu_d mg\cos\theta$. The diagram shows a block at rest on a 30° slope.

figure.alt: A block at rest on a rough slope inclined at 30 degrees. Weight W points straight down, normal force N points perpendicular to the slope, and friction Ff points up the slope, with length half that of the weight.

check.stem: A block rests on a plane whose tilt is slowly increased. The coefficient of static friction is 0.60. At what angle to the horizontal does the block start to slide?

options.why_wrong: This is correct: $\tan\theta = 0.60$.
This comes from $\sin\theta = 0.60$, but the condition is $\tan\theta = \mu_s$.
This comes from $\cos\theta = 0.60$, which is not the sliding condition.
This treats the coefficient 0.60 as an angle in degrees; $\mu_s$ has no units.

check.feedback_right: Sliding begins when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.60) = 31°$.
check.feedback_wrong: At the point of slipping $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\tan\theta = \mu_s = 0.60$ and $\theta = 31°$.

worked_example.problem: A crate of mass 12 kg rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients of friction are $\mu_s$ = 0.55 and $\mu_d$ = 0.40. Take g = 9.81 m s^-2. (a) Calculate the smallest horizontal force that makes the crate start to move. (b) Calculate the horizontal force needed to keep it moving at constant speed. (c) Calculate the acceleration of the crate when a horizontal force of 60 N acts on it while it slides.
steps: Normal force on a horizontal floor: $F_N = mg = 12 \times 9.81 = 117.7$ N.
(a) The crate starts to move when the push exceeds the maximum static friction: $\mu_s F_N = 0.55 \times 117.7 = 64.7$ N.
(b) At constant speed the resultant force is zero, so the push equals dynamic friction: $\mu_d F_N = 0.40 \times 117.7 = 47.1$ N.
(c) Resultant force = 60 − 47.1 = 12.9 N.
Acceleration: $a = F/m = 12.9/12 = 1.08$ m s^-2.

mistakes: Using $F_f = \mu_s F_N$ for any body at rest. Fix: static friction only equals $\mu_s F_N$ when the body is about to slip; otherwise it equals the force trying to move the body.
Using $F_N = mg$ on a slope. Fix: $F_N$ balances the force components perpendicular to the surface, so on an incline $F_N = mg\cos\theta$.
Using $\mu_s$ for a sliding body. Fix: once the body moves use $\mu_d$, which is usually smaller.
Thinking friction always points backwards. Fix: friction opposes motion relative to the surface, so it can act in the direction a body is accelerating, as with a walking person.

key_terms.definition: The component of the contact force acting perpendicular to the surface.
The component of the contact force parallel to the plane of contact, opposing relative sliding or the tendency to slide.
Friction on a body that is not sliding; it adjusts to the applied force up to a maximum of $\mu_s F_N$.
Friction on a sliding body, given by $F_f = \mu_d F_N$.
$\mu_s$, the ratio of maximum static friction to the normal force; it has no units.
$\mu_d$, the ratio of dynamic friction to the normal force; it has no units.

cards.front: What is the normal force?
cards.back: The component of the contact force perpendicular to the surface, which counteracts the body pressing into the surface.

cards.front: What is the frictional force?
cards.back: The component of the contact force parallel to the surface, opposing the relative sliding or tendency to slide of the body.

cards.front: Equation for static friction
cards.back: $F_f \le \mu_s F_N$. Static friction adjusts to the applied force up to a maximum of $\mu_s F_N$.

cards.front: Equation for dynamic friction
cards.back: $F_f = \mu_d F_N$ for a body that is sliding.

cards.front: Units of $\mu_s$ and $\mu_d$

cards.front: How do $\mu_s$ and $\mu_d$ usually compare?
cards.back: $\mu_d < \mu_s$ for most surfaces, so it takes more force to start a body moving than to keep it moving.

cards.front: A block at rest is pushed with a force smaller than $\mu_s F_N$. What is friction?
cards.back: Equal and opposite to the push, since the block is in equilibrium.

cards.front: When does $F_f = \mu_s F_N$ exactly?
cards.back: Only when the body is on the point of slipping.

cards.front: Normal force on a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces

cards.front: Normal force on a slope of angle $\theta$
cards.back: $F_N = mg\cos\theta$.

body.intro: Hooke's law describes the restoring force a spring exerts when it is stretched or compressed: the force is proportional to the extension. It matters because springs, cables and many other elastic objects follow this rule, and it is the starting point for simple harmonic motion and elastic energy.

sections.heading: The elastic restoring force
sections.body: When you stretch or compress a spring, it pulls or pushes back. This elastic restoring force tries to return the spring to its natural length. Hooke's law says that, for small deformations, the force is proportional to the extension $x$, which is the change from natural length: $F_H = -kx$. The constant $k$ is the spring constant and measures how stiff the spring is. The minus sign shows that the force acts in the opposite direction to the displacement. If the spring is stretched to the right, the force on whatever stretches it points left. The magnitude is simply $F = kx$. Note that $x$ is the extension from natural length, not the total length of the spring. Doubling the extension doubles the force.

check.stem: A spring is stretched to the right. What does the minus sign in $F_H = -kx$ tell you?

options.text: The force on the stretcher points to the left, opposite to the extension
options.why_wrong: This is the correct statement.
k is always positive; the minus sign belongs to the direction of the force, not to k.
Extension can be positive (stretch) or negative (compression); the sign is not fixed.

options.text: The force gets smaller as the spring is stretched
options.why_wrong: The magnitude of the force increases with extension; the minus sign gives direction only.

check.feedback_right: Yes, the minus sign means the restoring force opposes the displacement.
check.feedback_wrong: The minus sign is about direction: the restoring force always points back towards the natural length, opposite to the extension. The magnitude is $kx$.

sections.heading: The spring constant
sections.body: Rearranging $F = kx$ gives $k = \frac{F}{x}$. The spring constant is the force needed per unit extension, so its unit is newtons per metre, N m^-1. A large $k$ means a stiff spring: a big force produces only a small extension. A small $k$ means a soft spring. Always convert extensions to metres before calculating. For example, an extension of 5.0 cm is 0.050 m. If a force of 10 N produces an extension of 0.20 m, then $k = \frac{10}{0.20} = 50$ N m^-1. The same spring will then give 5.0 N for 0.10 m, 15 N for 0.30 m, and so on, as long as Hooke's law is obeyed.

check.stem: A force of 8.0 N extends a spring by 0.050 m. Calculate the spring constant in N m^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Use $k = F/x$ with $x$ in metres. Typing 0.0063 comes from dividing $x$ by $F$ (inverted the formula), and 400 comes from using $x$ = 0.020 m by mistake. Here $k = 8.0/0.050 = 160$ N m^-1.

sections.heading: Reading the force-extension graph
sections.body: A graph of force against extension shows how a spring behaves. The graph in the figure is a straight line through the origin for small forces, which is Hooke's law. The gradient of the straight section equals the spring constant $k$. Beyond a certain point the line curves. This point is the limit of proportionality. Past it, the extension is no longer proportional to the force, so $F = -kx$ does not apply. Stretch the spring far enough and it will no longer return to its original length: it has passed its elastic limit. To find $k$, pick two points on the straight section far apart and calculate $\frac{\Delta F}{\Delta x}$. Do not use points on the curved part.

figure.alt: Graph of force F in newtons against extension x in metres for a spring. The points lie on a straight line through the origin from x = 0 to x = 0.10 m, where F = 5.0 N. Beyond that, the line bends towards the extension axis, reaching F = 5.6 N at x = 0.12 m and F = 5.9 N at x = 0.14 m.

sections.heading: A hanging mass in equilibrium
sections.body: When a mass hangs at rest from a vertical spring, the forces on it balance. The weight $mg$ acts down and the elastic force $kx$ acts up. By Newton's first law the resultant is zero, so $kx = mg$ and the extension is $x = \frac{mg}{k}$. This is a common IB situation. Adding more mass increases the extension in proportion, provided the spring stays within its limit of proportionality. Note that $x$ is measured from the natural length of the spring, not from the position where the spring hung with a previous load. If a second mass is added, the extra extension depends only on the extra weight.

check.stem: A mass of 0.50 kg hangs at rest from a spring of spring constant 100 N m^-1. Calculate the extension of the spring in metres. Use g = 9.81 N kg^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Set $kx = mg$. Typing 0.005 comes from leaving out g (using $m/k$), and 20 comes from inverting to $k/(mg)$. Here $x = 4.905/100 = 0.049$ m.

Extension $x = \frac{2.943}{40} = 0.0736$ m, so about 0.074 m.

The total mass needed is 0.60 kg, so the extra mass is 0.30 kg.

Leaving the extension in cm. Fix: convert to metres before using $k$ in N m^-1.
Using points on the curved part of the graph to find $k$. Fix: use only the straight section, where Hooke's law holds.
Forgetting that the weight is $mg$, not just $m$. Fix: multiply the mass by 9.81 N kg^-1 to get the force in newtons.

body.intro: Circular motion is motion along a curved path, where a resultant force towards the centre keeps changing the direction of the velocity. It explains how cars turn, how satellites orbit and how charged particles move in magnetic fields.

sections.heading: Velocity changes even at constant speed
sections.body: Velocity is a vector, so it changes if its direction changes, even when the speed stays the same. A body moving in a circle at constant speed therefore accelerates. At every instant the velocity points along the tangent to the circle, while the change in velocity points towards the centre. This means the acceleration is directed radially inward and is called centripetal acceleration. By Newton's second law, a resultant force must act in the same direction as the acceleration, so it too points to the centre. This is the centripetal force. It acts at right angles to the velocity, so it changes direction but does no work and does not change the speed.

check.stem: A ball moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which statement about its acceleration is correct?

options.text: It is zero because the speed is constant.
options.why_wrong: Velocity is a vector; a change of direction is still an acceleration.

options.text: It is directed towards the centre of the circle.
options.why_wrong: This is correct.

options.text: It is directed along the tangent, in the direction of motion.
options.why_wrong: An acceleration along the velocity would change the speed, which stays constant.

options.text: It is directed away from the centre of the circle.
options.why_wrong: This confuses the acceleration with the outward 'centrifugal' effect felt in the rotating frame.

check.feedback_right: Yes, the velocity changes direction towards the centre, so the acceleration points inward.
check.feedback_wrong: Speed is constant but direction changes, so there is an acceleration. It is perpendicular to the velocity and points to the centre.

sections.heading: Describing the motion: period, speed and angular velocity
sections.body: One full circle takes the period $T$. The linear speed is the circumference divided by the period: $v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$. The angular velocity $\omega$ is the angle swept per unit time, in rad s^-1, with $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$. Combining these gives $v = \omega r$. The frequency is $f = \frac{1}{T}$, so $\omega = 2\pi f$. Points on a rotating disc all have the same $\omega$, but points further from the axis have a greater linear speed $v$ because $v = \omega r$. Always use radians when working with $\omega$.

check.stem: A wheel rotates with a period of 0.50 s. Calculate its angular velocity in rad s^-1 to 3 significant figures.
check.feedback_right: Correct: $\omega = 2\pi / 0.50 = 12.6$ rad s^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Use $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ with $T = 0.50$ s. Dividing 1 by T gives the frequency, 2.0 Hz, not $\omega$.

sections.heading: Centripetal acceleration and force
sections.body: The centripetal acceleration has magnitude $a = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2}$. Applying $F = ma$ gives the centripetal force $F = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$. Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is the name for the resultant of real forces pointing to the centre: tension for a ball on a string, friction for a car on a flat bend, gravity for a satellite, the normal force and weight combined for a vehicle on a hill. Doubling the speed at fixed radius needs four times the force, since $F \propto v^2$. If the force vanishes, the body moves off along the tangent in a straight line, by Newton's first law.

sections.heading: Vertical circles and non-uniform motion
sections.body: In a vertical circle, weight acts downwards at every point, so the speed is not constant and the motion is non-uniform. You only need the top and the bottom. The resultant force towards the centre equals $\frac{mv^2}{r}$ in both cases. At the bottom, tension $T$ points up to the centre and weight down, so $T - mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$. At the top, both tension and weight point towards the centre, so $T + mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$. The tension is therefore greatest at the bottom. At the top, the minimum speed occurs when $T = 0$, giving $v = \sqrt{gr}$. The speed is greatest at the bottom and least at the top, as kinetic energy changes into gravitational potential energy.

body.intro: Linear momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity, and an impulse is the push that changes it. These ideas explain how to predict the effect of a force acting for a short time, as in a bat hitting a ball or a car crumpling in a crash.

sections.heading: Linear momentum
sections.body: Linear momentum $p$ measures how hard it is to stop a moving object. It is defined as $p = mv$, where $m$ is the mass in kg and $v$ the velocity in m s^-1. The unit is kg m s^-1, which is the same as N s. Momentum is a vector, so it points in the direction of the velocity. A 1000 kg car and a 10 kg bicycle can have the same momentum if the bicycle moves 100 times faster. Momentum stays constant unless a resultant external force acts on the object. Choose one direction as positive, and give motion in the opposite direction a negative sign. The idea that total momentum is conserved in a system has its own lesson. Here we focus on how a single object's momentum changes.

check.stem: A ball of mass 0.40 kg moves at 5.0 m s^-1. What is its momentum?

options.why_wrong: This is the correct value, 0.40 × 5.0.
This divides mass by speed (0.40 / 5.0) instead of multiplying.
This divides speed by mass (5.0 / 0.40) instead of multiplying.
This uses the kinetic energy form $\frac{1}{2}mv$ and wrongly includes a factor of one half.

check.feedback_right: Correct: p = mv = 0.40 × 5.0 = 2.0 kg m s^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, with no factor of one half. So p = 0.40 × 5.0 = 2.0 kg m s^-1.

sections.heading: Impulse equals change in momentum
sections.body: When a resultant external force $F$ acts on a body for a time $\Delta t$, it delivers an impulse $J = F\Delta t$. Here $F$ is the average resultant force and $\Delta t$ is the time of contact. The unit of impulse is N s. The applied impulse equals the change in momentum of the body: $J = F\Delta t = \Delta p = mv - mu$, where $u$ is the initial velocity and $v$ the final velocity. A bigger force or a longer contact time gives a bigger change in momentum. Impulse is a vector in the direction of the resultant force. Remember that the force must be the resultant force. If other forces act too, they must be included.

check.stem: A constant resultant force of 8.0 N acts on a body for 0.50 s. Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the body, in kg m s^-1.
check.feedback_right: Correct: Δp = FΔt = 8.0 × 0.50 = 4.0 kg m s^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: The change in momentum equals the impulse, which is force multiplied by time. So Δp = 8.0 × 0.50 = 4.0 kg m s^-1.

sections.heading: Force-time graphs
sections.body: In real impacts the force is not constant. It rises to a peak and falls back to zero. A force-time graph shows this. The area under the graph equals the impulse, and so the change in momentum. For a triangle, area = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ height. In the graph, a ball initially at rest is kicked. The force rises from zero to a maximum and falls to zero over 0.020 s. The area is the impulse delivered. Dividing the impulse by the mass gives the change in velocity, since $\Delta v = \frac{J}{m}$.

figure.alt: Force-time graph for a kick. The force rises in a straight line from 0 N at 0 s to 60 N at 0.010 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 N at 0.020 s, forming a triangle.

check.stem: The graph shows the force on a ball of mass 0.30 kg, initially at rest. Calculate the speed of the ball after the kick, in m s^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Find the area of the triangle, ½ × 0.020 × 60 = 0.60 N s. This is the impulse, so v = J / m = 0.60 / 0.30 = 2.0 m s^-1.

sections.heading: Newton's second law as rate of change of momentum
sections.body: Dividing $J = \Delta p$ by the time gives $F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$. This is Newton's second law in its more general form: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum. The familiar $F = ma$ only works when the mass is constant. $F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$ also works when mass changes, for example sand falling onto a moving conveyor belt or a rocket burning fuel. It also explains safety features. Crumple zones, airbags and bending your knees on landing all increase the contact time $\Delta t$. For the same $\Delta p$, a longer time means a smaller average force, so there is less damage or injury.

body.intro: Conservation of linear momentum says that the total momentum of a system stays constant unless a resultant external force acts on it. It lets us predict the motion of colliding or exploding bodies without knowing the detailed forces between them.

sections.heading: Momentum and isolated systems
sections.body: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$. It is a vector, so direction matters: choose one direction as positive and give the opposite direction a negative sign. Its unit is kg m s^-1 (equivalent to N s). A system is isolated when no resultant external force acts on it. For an isolated system the total momentum is constant. This follows from Newton's laws, because the forces between two interacting bodies are equal and opposite and act for the same time, so one body gains exactly the momentum the other loses. Friction with the ground or a push from outside is an external force and would change the total. Internal forces, such as the force between colliding trolleys, never change the total momentum of the system.

options.why_wrong: This is correct.

options.why_wrong: Internal forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel in the total.

Total momentum is conserved, not zeroed, unless it started as zero.

check.feedback_right: With no resultant external force, internal forces cancel and the total momentum is constant.
check.feedback_wrong: Forces between the bodies are equal and opposite for the same time, so the changes in momentum cancel. Total momentum is constant.

sections.heading: Using conservation in one dimension
sections.body: To use the principle, write total momentum before equals total momentum after: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$. Choose a positive direction first. A body moving the other way has a negative velocity. For a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together, so after the collision $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1+m_2)v$. For example, a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s^-1 hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick. Momentum before is 6.0 kg m s^-1, so the final speed is $ rac{6.0}{3.0} = 2.0$ m s^-1 in the original direction. The method needs only the masses and velocities, not the force or the collision time.

sections.heading: Explosions and recoil
sections.body: In an explosion, a body initially at rest splits into parts. Total momentum before is zero, so the total after must also be zero: $m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = 0$. The parts move in opposite directions, and the lighter part has the greater speed. For example, a 4.0 kg cannon fires a 1.0 kg shell at 20 m s^-1. Then $4.0v + 1.0 \times 20 = 0$, so the cannon recoils at 5.0 m s^-1 in the opposite direction. Kinetic energy is not conserved here: it increases because stored chemical or elastic energy is transferred to kinetic energy. Momentum is still conserved. This is the same reason a rocket speeds up as it expels gas backwards.

sections.heading: Momentum and energy in collisions
sections.body: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system, but kinetic energy is not always. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved, and the bodies separate. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy, sound or deformation. The loss is greatest when the bodies stick together. Compare two trolleys: a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m s^-1 hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick, moving at 2.0 m s^-1. Kinetic energy before is $\frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 3.0^2 = 9.0$ J. After it is $\frac{1}{2} \times 3.0 \times 2.0^2 = 6.0$ J. So 3.0 J is lost, yet momentum was 6.0 kg m s^-1 both before and after. Always check the energy to classify a collision.

body.intro: An elastic collision conserves kinetic energy, while an inelastic collision transfers some kinetic energy to other forms such as thermal energy and sound. Knowing which type has occurred lets you predict speeds after impact and calculate how much energy is lost.

sections.heading: Two kinds of collision
sections.body:
In any collision between two bodies in an isolated system, total momentum is the same before and after (this is covered in its own lesson, so here we simply use it). What distinguishes collisions is what happens to kinetic energy, $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

In an **elastic collision** the total kinetic energy after equals the total kinetic energy before. Nothing is permanently transferred to thermal energy, sound or deformation. Collisions between gas molecules are close to elastic.

In an **inelastic collision** the total kinetic energy after is less than before. The missing energy becomes thermal energy, sound or permanent deformation. Most everyday collisions, such as a car crash or a ball of clay hitting the floor, are inelastic.

Total energy is always conserved. Only the kinetic part can fall.

Total energy is always conserved; only kinetic energy is transferred to other forms.

options.text: Total kinetic energy stays the same
options.why_wrong: That describes an elastic collision.

check.feedback_right: Kinetic energy falls but the lost energy appears as thermal energy, sound or deformation, so total energy is conserved.
check.feedback_wrong: Inelastic means kinetic energy is not conserved, but total energy always is. The lost kinetic energy goes into thermal energy, sound or deformation.

sections.heading: Testing a collision with kinetic energy
sections.body:
To decide whether a collision is elastic, calculate the total kinetic energy before and after and compare them.

Step 1: find $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ for each body before, and add.
Step 2: do the same after.
Step 3: if the totals are equal, the collision is elastic. If the total is smaller, it is inelastic.

The energy transferred is

$\Delta E = E_{k,before} - E_{k,after}$

The table gives an example: a 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s^-1 hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. In case A they bounce apart, and in case B they stick together. Use the data to compare the total kinetic energy in each case.

Speed of 1.0 kg trolley after / m s^-1

sections.heading: Elastic collisions and relative speed
sections.body:
For a collision in one dimension that is elastic, the bodies separate at the same speed at which they approached:

$\text{speed of approach} = \text{speed of separation}$

This is a quick test. In case A of the table, the 2.0 kg trolley moves at 3.0 m s^-1 towards a stationary trolley, so the approach speed is 3.0 m s^-1. Afterwards the speeds are 1.0 and 4.0 m s^-1 in the same direction, so the separation speed is 4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0 m s^-1. They match, so the collision is elastic.

Check with energy: after, $\frac{1}{2}(2.0)(1.0)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(1.0)(4.0)^2 = 1.0 + 8.0 = 9.0$ J, equal to the 9.0 J before. Elastic collisions are an idealisation, but ones between hard steel balls or gas molecules come very close.

check.feedback_wrong: Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy, which in one dimension means separation speed equals approach speed, so 5.0 m s^-1.

sections.heading: Inelastic collisions and energy loss
sections.body:
In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms, so the separation speed is less than the approach speed.

A **completely inelastic** collision is one in which the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity. This gives the largest possible loss of kinetic energy for the collision. All the kinetic energy is lost only if the combined body ends at rest, which happens only when the total momentum was zero.

In case B of the table, the trolleys stick together. Before: 9.0 J. After: 6.0 J. The energy transferred is

$\Delta E = 9.0 - 6.0 = 3.0$ J

The fraction of kinetic energy lost is $\frac{3.0}{9.0} = 0.33$. This energy appears as thermal energy and sound in the trolleys.

check.feedback_wrong: Sticking together is completely inelastic, so kinetic energy falls. It is all lost only if the combined body stops, so a moving combined body still has some.

worked_example.problem: A 0.60 kg trolley moving at 2.0 m s^-1 collides with a stationary 0.40 kg trolley. They stick together and move off at 1.2 m s^-1. Determine the kinetic energy transferred to other forms in the collision.
steps: Kinetic energy before: (1/2)(0.60)(2.0)^2 = 1.2 J (the second trolley is at rest, so contributes 0).
Total mass after = 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.0 kg.
Kinetic energy after: (1/2)(1.0)(1.2)^2 = 0.72 J.
Energy transferred = 1.2 - 0.72 = 0.48 J.
worked_example.answer: 0.48 J, transferred to thermal energy and sound, so the collision is inelastic.

Thinking sticking together means all kinetic energy is lost. Fix: kinetic energy is all lost only if the combined body is at rest; otherwise it still has some.

lessons.subtopic: Kinetic, gravitational and elastic potential energy

body.intro: Mechanical energy is stored or carried in three main ways: motion (kinetic), height in a gravitational field (gravitational potential) and stretch or compression (elastic potential). Knowing the equation for each lets you predict speeds, heights and extensions without tracking forces through time.

sections.heading: Kinetic energy: energy of motion
sections.body:
Any object that is moving has kinetic energy. For translational motion, $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, where $m$ is the mass in kg and $v$ is the speed in m s^-1. The energy is in joules (J). Because $v$ is squared, doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times larger. Kinetic energy is never negative, and it does not depend on the direction of motion.

Momentum is $p = mv$. Substituting $v = p/m$ gives an equivalent form: $E_k = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. This form is useful when a question gives momentum instead of speed.

check.stem: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s^-1. Give your answer in J.
check.feedback_right: Correct: $\frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 3.0^2 = 9.0$ J.
check.feedback_wrong: Square only the speed, then multiply by half the mass: $\frac{1}{2}\times 2.0\times 9.0 = 9.0$ J. Using $mv$ gives 6.0, which is the momentum, not the energy.

sections.heading: Gravitational potential energy near Earth
sections.body:
An object raised in a gravitational field gains gravitational potential energy. Close to the Earth's surface, where $g$ is effectively constant, the change is $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$. Here $m$ is the mass, $g = 9.81$ N kg^-1 (or m s^-2) and $\Delta h$ is the change in vertical height.

Only the vertical change matters. Carrying a box 10 m along a level floor changes $E_p$ by zero. Raising it 2 m changes $E_p$ by $mg \times 2$, however it gets there. The equation is for small height changes only, because $g$ falls as you move far from the surface. Far from Earth a different expression is needed.

check.stem: Calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy of a 0.50 kg book lifted vertically through 2.0 m. Use g = 9.81 N kg^-1. Give your answer in J to two significant figures.
check.feedback_right: Correct: $0.50 \times 9.81 \times 2.0 = 9.8$ J.
check.feedback_wrong: Multiply mass, $g$ and the height change: $0.50\times 9.81\times 2.0 = 9.8$ J. Do not square anything or halve it.

sections.heading: Elastic potential energy in a spring
sections.body:
A stretched or compressed spring stores elastic potential energy. For a spring that obeys Hooke's law, $F = k\Delta x$, where $k$ is the spring constant in N m^-1 and $\Delta x$ is the extension or compression from its natural length. The stored energy is $E_H = \frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2$.

The formula comes from the graph of force against extension. The work done stretching the spring equals the area under the line, which is a triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times \Delta x \times F = \frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2$. Because the extension is squared, doubling it stores four times the energy.

figure.alt: Graph of force in newtons against extension in metres for a spring. A straight line through the origin passes through (0.10, 5.0) and (0.20, 10.0).

check.stem: Use the area under the graph to determine the energy stored in the spring at an extension of 0.20 m. Give your answer in J.
check.feedback_right: Correct: area $= \frac{1}{2}\times 0.20\times 10.0 = 1.0$ J.
check.feedback_wrong: The area is a triangle, so use $\frac{1}{2}\times$ base $\times$ height $= \frac{1}{2}\times 0.20\times 10.0 = 1.0$ J. Using base $\times$ height gives 2.0 J, which is double the true value.

sections.heading: Swapping between the three forms
sections.body:
In many situations energy changes from one mechanical form to another. If friction and air resistance are absent, the total mechanical energy $E_k + E_p$ (gravitational plus elastic) stays constant. This idea is covered in detail in the conservation of energy lesson. Here we use it to link the three equations.

A ball dropped from rest loses gravitational potential energy and gains the same amount of kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg\Delta h$. The mass cancels, so $v = \sqrt{2g\Delta h}$. In the same way, a compressed spring that pushes a block along a smooth surface turns elastic energy into kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

check.stem: A ball is dropped from rest and falls 1.8 m. Air resistance is negligible. What is its speed just before it lands? Use g = 9.81 m s^-2.

options.why_wrong: This is $2g\Delta h$; the square root was not taken.
This is $\sqrt{g\Delta h}$; the factor of 2 was left out.
This is $g\Delta h$; the factor 2 and the square root were both omitted.

check.feedback_right: Correct: $v=\sqrt{2\times 9.81\times 1.8}=5.9$ m s^-1.
check.feedback_wrong: Set $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg\Delta h$, so $v=\sqrt{2g\Delta h}=\sqrt{35.3}=5.9$ m s^-1.

worked_example.problem: A block of mass 0.20 kg rests against a horizontal spring of spring constant 200 N m^-1. The spring is compressed by 0.050 m and released. The surface is smooth. Calculate the speed of the block as it leaves the spring.
steps: Elastic energy stored: $E_H=\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2=\frac{1}{2}\times 200\times 0.050^2=0.25$ J.
The surface is smooth, so all of this becomes kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2=0.25$ J.
Rearrange: $v^2=\frac{2\times 0.25}{0.20}=2.5$.
Take the square root: $v=1.58$ m s^-1.

mistakes: Forgetting to square the speed or the extension. Fix: in $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2$ only $v$ and $\Delta x$ are squared, never the whole bracket.
Using the length of the path instead of the vertical height in $mg\Delta h$. Fix: measure only the vertical change in height.
Using the total length of a spring instead of its extension from natural length. Fix: $\Delta x$ is the stretch or compression, not the whole length.
Leaving out the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in kinetic or elastic energy. Fix: write the equation out before substituting.

body.intro: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, and efficiency tells us what fraction of the energy put in ends up doing something useful. These ideas let us compare machines, size motors and judge how wasteful a device is.

sections.heading: Power as a rate
sections.body: Power measures how fast energy is transferred. If work $\Delta W$ is done in a time $\Delta t$, the power is $P = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$. The unit is the watt, W, where 1 W = 1 J s^-1. A 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of electrical energy every second. Two machines can do the same work, but the more powerful one does it in less time. Rearranging gives $\Delta W = P\Delta t$, so energy transferred is power multiplied by time. Always convert time to seconds and kilowatts to watts before calculating.

check.stem: A motor transfers 4800 J of energy in 12 s. Calculate its power in W.
check.feedback_wrong: Power is energy divided by time, $P = \Delta W/\Delta t$. Here 4800 J / 12 s = 400 W.

sections.heading: Power, force and velocity
sections.body: When a constant force $F$ moves an object at constant speed $v$ along the line of the force, the work done in time $\Delta t$ is $F s = F v \Delta t$. Dividing by $\Delta t$ gives $P = Fv$. This is useful for vehicles: a car travelling at constant speed has a driving force equal to the resistive force, so the engine power needed is the resistive force multiplied by the speed. At a fixed power, a larger speed means a smaller force. This is why a vehicle going up a steep hill slows down if the engine power stays the same. Use speed in m s^-1 and force in N to get power in W.

check.stem: A cyclist moves at a constant 8.0 m s^-1 against a total resistive force of 25 N. What power does the cyclist develop?

options.why_wrong: Divided speed by force (8.0/25 is about 0.32, and 25/8.0 = 3.1) instead of multiplying.
Added force and speed (25 + 8.0) instead of multiplying.
This is not applicable: it is correct.
Squared the speed and multiplied by force (25 × 64 = 1600).

check.feedback_right: Yes: $P = Fv = 25 \times 8.0 = 200$ W.
check.feedback_wrong: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so $P = Fv = 25 \times 8.0 = 200$ W.

sections.heading: Efficiency
sections.body: No real device transfers all its input energy into the useful form. Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to total input: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful work out}}{\text{total work in}} = \frac{\text{useful power out}}{\text{total power in}}$. It has no unit and is between 0 and 1, or between 0% and 100% when multiplied by 100. The rest of the energy is wasted, usually as thermal energy, but it is not destroyed. So input = useful output + wasted energy. A lamp with an efficiency of 0.15 turns 15% of its electrical input into light. Always put the useful quantity on top.

check.stem: A device takes in 500 J of energy and transfers 125 J usefully. What is its efficiency?

options.why_wrong: This is not applicable: it is correct.
Inverted the ratio (500/125); efficiency cannot exceed 1.
Used the wasted fraction (375/500) instead of the useful fraction.
Added the two energies instead of dividing.

check.feedback_wrong: Efficiency = useful out / total in = 125/500 = 0.25, never more than 1.

sections.heading: Efficiency of a lifting machine
sections.body: Efficiency questions often combine power with other quantities. A motor lifts a load at constant speed. The useful power output is the rate at which gravitational potential energy increases, $\frac{mg\Delta h}{\Delta t} = mgv$. The input power is the electrical power supplied, $VI$. Then $\eta = \frac{mgv}{P_{in}}$. A hoist raising a 200 kg load at 0.50 m s^-1 gives useful power 200 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 981 W. If the motor draws 1400 W, then $\eta = 981/1400 = 0.70$. The wasted power, 419 W, appears mostly as thermal energy in the motor and friction in the machine.

check.stem: A motor draws 800 W and lifts a 40 kg mass at a constant 1.0 m s^-1. Use g = 9.81 m s^-2. Calculate the efficiency as a decimal to 2 significant figures.
check.feedback_right: Correct: useful power = 40 × 9.81 × 1.0 = 392 W, and 392/800 = 0.49.
check.feedback_wrong: Useful output power is $mgv = 392$ W, so $\eta = 392/800 = 0.49$.

worked_example.problem: A car of resistive force 600 N travels at a constant 25 m s^-1. Its engine takes in chemical energy at a rate of 60 kW. Calculate (a) the useful power developed to overcome the resistive force and (b) the efficiency of the engine.
steps: At constant speed, driving force = resistive force = 600 N.
Useful power $P = Fv = 600 \times 25 = 15000$ W = 15 kW.
Total power in = 60 kW.
Efficiency $\eta = 15/60 = 0.25$.

mistakes: Using kilowatts, minutes or hours without converting: convert to W and s before using $P = \Delta W/\Delta t$.
Putting the wasted energy on top of the efficiency ratio: efficiency is useful out divided by total in.
Using $P = Fv$ when the speed is not constant or the force is not along the motion: for constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force.
Quoting efficiency with a unit or above 1: it is a ratio, at most 1 (or 100%).

body.intro: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another, and a Sankey diagram shows these transfers as arrows whose widths are proportional to the amounts of energy. Reading and drawing them lets you find useful output, wasted energy and efficiency for any device.

sections.heading: Energy is conserved
sections.body: The principle of conservation of energy says the total energy of an isolated system stays constant. Energy is never lost; it is transferred between stores (kinetic, thermal, electrical, chemical, gravitational and so on) or dissipated to the surroundings. When a force does work on a system, that work is a transfer of energy. Energy is measured in joules (J). In a real device some energy ends up in a form we do not want, usually thermal energy spread into the surroundings. We call this wasted (dissipated) energy. The energy is still there, but it is no longer useful. For any device, total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy out.

check.stem: A motor takes in 500 J of electrical energy and transfers 380 J usefully as kinetic energy. What happens to the other 120 J?

options.why_wrong: Energy is conserved, so it cannot be destroyed.

options.text: It is dissipated, mainly as thermal energy to the surroundings
options.why_wrong: This is correct.

options.text: It is stored in the motor as extra kinetic energy
options.why_wrong: The 380 J already counts the kinetic energy output; the rest is not kinetic.
Dissipated energy spreads out and is not usefully recovered.

check.feedback_right: Energy is conserved, so the missing 120 J is dissipated, mainly as thermal energy.
check.feedback_wrong: Energy is never destroyed. Whatever is not useful output is wasted energy, usually thermal, spread into the surroundings.

sections.heading: Reading a Sankey diagram
sections.body: A Sankey diagram shows energy transfers as arrows. The input arrow enters on the left. It splits into a useful output arrow that continues forward and wasted energy arrows that branch off, often upwards or downwards. The width of each arrow is drawn to the same scale as its energy, so a 100 J arrow is twice as wide as a 50 J arrow. Because energy is conserved, the widths of the outputs add up to the width of the input. Each arrow should be labelled with its energy value and the form of energy. The diagram below shows a lamp: 200 J enters as electrical energy, 30 J leaves as light and 170 J as thermal energy.

figure.alt: Bar chart of energy for a lamp: electrical input 200 J, useful light output 30 J, wasted thermal output 170 J. Sankey arrow widths would be in these proportions.

check.stem: The chart gives the energy values that a Sankey diagram for the lamp would show. If the input arrow is drawn 20 mm wide, how wide is the thermal arrow?

options.why_wrong: This is the width of the light arrow (30 J), not the thermal arrow.
This is correct.
This would mean all the energy is wasted, which is the input width.
This uses 1 mm per joule, ignoring the scale set by the 20 mm input.

check.feedback_right: The scale is 20 mm per 200 J, so 170 J is 17 mm.
check.feedback_wrong: Find the scale first: 20 mm per 200 J is 0.1 mm per joule. Multiply by 170 J to get 17 mm.

sections.heading: Using a Sankey diagram to find efficiency
sections.body: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the input energy is transferred usefully: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful energy out}}{\text{total energy in}}$. It has no units and lies between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). Using power instead of energy gives the same ratio: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful power out}}{\text{total power in}}$. On a Sankey diagram this is the width of the useful arrow divided by the width of the input arrow. For the lamp with 200 J in and 30 J of light, $\eta = \frac{30}{200} = 0.15$, or 15%. No real device is 100% efficient, because some energy is always dissipated. You can also find a missing value: wasted energy = total in − useful out.

check.stem: A device takes in 800 J of energy and wastes 600 J as thermal energy. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.
check.feedback_right: Useful energy is 800 − 600 = 200 J, so efficiency is 200/800 = 0.25.
check.feedback_wrong: Subtract the wasted energy from the input to get the useful energy (200 J), then divide by the input 800 J.

sections.heading: Chains of transfers
sections.body: Many systems have several stages, and a Sankey diagram can show each one. For example, a power station burns fuel (chemical energy), heats steam, turns turbines and drives generators. Some energy is wasted at every stage. For stages in series, the overall efficiency is the product of the individual efficiencies: $\eta_{total} = \eta_1 \times \eta_2$. If stage 1 is 80% efficient and stage 2 is 50% efficient, the overall efficiency is $0.80 \times 0.50 = 0.40$, or 40%. Notice that the overall efficiency is lower than either stage. The energy density of a fuel, energy released per unit mass or volume, tells you how much input energy a given amount of fuel provides, and so how much useful output you can expect.

check.stem: Two machines in series have efficiencies of 0.90 and 0.60. Calculate the overall efficiency as a decimal.
check.feedback_right: Overall efficiency is 0.90 × 0.60 = 0.54.
check.feedback_wrong: Efficiencies in series are multiplied, not added or averaged: 0.90 × 0.60 = 0.54.

worked_example.problem: A wind turbine receives 4.0 MJ of kinetic energy from the wind each second. 1.0 MJ is lost as thermal energy in the blades and gearbox, and a further 0.6 MJ is lost as thermal energy in the generator. Determine the useful electrical energy produced per second and the efficiency of the turbine.
steps: Total wasted energy = 1.0 + 0.6 = 1.6 MJ.
Useful energy out = total in − wasted = 4.0 − 1.6 = 2.4 MJ.
Efficiency = useful out / total in = 2.4 / 4.0 = 0.60.
On a Sankey diagram the useful arrow would be 60% of the input width.
worked_example.answer: Useful electrical energy = 2.4 MJ per second; efficiency = 0.60 (60%).

mistakes: Adding efficiencies of stages in series. Fix: multiply them.
Forgetting that arrow widths are drawn to scale. Fix: use one scale for every arrow, so outputs add up to the input width.
Saying wasted energy is 'lost' or destroyed. Fix: say it is dissipated, usually as thermal energy to the surroundings.
Dividing by the useful energy instead of the total input. Fix: efficiency = useful out / total in.

Energy transferred to forms that are not wanted, usually thermal energy in the surroundings.
The ratio of useful energy (or power) out to total energy (or power) in.
The energy released per unit mass or volume of a fuel.

cards.front: State the principle of conservation of energy.
cards.back: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total energy of an isolated system is constant. It is only transferred between stores.

cards.front: What is a Sankey diagram?
cards.back: A diagram of energy transfers using arrows whose widths are proportional to the energy transferred.

cards.front: What does arrow width show in a Sankey diagram?
cards.back: The amount of energy in that transfer, drawn to a common scale.

cards.front: In a Sankey diagram, how do output widths relate to the input width?
cards.back: The output widths (useful plus wasted) add up to the input width, because energy is conserved.

cards.front: What is wasted (dissipated) energy?
cards.back: Energy transferred to unwanted forms, usually thermal energy spread into the surroundings.

cards.front: What is useful energy?
cards.back: The part of the input energy transferred in the form that is wanted.

cards.front: Equation for wasted energy.
cards.back: Wasted energy = total energy in − useful energy out.

cards.front: Define efficiency.
cards.back: Useful energy (or power) out divided by total energy (or power) in.

cards.front: Efficiency equation in terms of energy.
cards.back: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful energy out}}{\text{total energy in}}$

cards.front: Efficiency equation in terms of power.
cards.back: $\eta = \frac{\text{useful power out}}{\text{total power in}}$

cards.front: Does efficiency have units?
cards.back: No. It is a ratio, between 0 and 1 or 0% to 100%.

cards.front: Can a real device have efficiency of 1?
cards.back: No. Some energy is always dissipated, so efficiency is less than 1.

cards.front: How do you combine efficiencies of stages in series?
cards.back: Multiply them: $\eta_{total} = \eta_1 \times \eta_2 \times \dots$

Unit of energy?
cards.back: The joule, J.

cards.front: Work done by a force relates to energy how?
cards.back: Work done by a force is equivalent to a transfer of energy.

cards.front: What is energy density?
cards.back: Energy released per unit mass (J kg^-1) or per unit volume (J m^-3) of a fuel.

cards.front: Where does most wasted energy end up?
cards.back: As thermal energy in the surroundings, where it is spread out and cannot be usefully recovered.
